elements.content: Communication Goal: I can name everyday objects, describe rooms and workspaces, use articles, and ask for things politely.

Lesson overview:
- Level: A0-A1 General English
- Unit: Inspired Module 2. Everyday Spaces
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: Everyday Spaces
- Materials: Real objects, cafe scene pictures, floor plan, request cards.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• name personal and work objects
• describe a room with there is/are
• ask for and borrow everyday items
Recycling & Course Continuity:

Prior learning: Recycles personal details and greetings.

Next lesson: Lesson 3 recycles objects and places to talk about daily routines.
Quick retrieval task: which words or phrases do you remember?
Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (15 items):

laptop — a portable computer. Example: My laptop is in my bag.
charger — a cable or device that charges a battery. Example: Can I borrow a charger?
headphones — devices for listening to sound. Example: My headphones are on the desk.
notebook — a book for writing notes. Example: I write in my notebook.
keys — small objects that open doors. Example: The keys are on the table.
wallet — a small case for money and cards. Example: My wallet is in my bag.
bottle — a container for water or other drinks. Example: I have a water bottle.
glasses — lenses you wear to see better. Example: My glasses are on the table.
phone — a mobile or telephone. Example: My phone is in my bag.
ID card — a card that shows who you are. Example: This is my ID card.
coffee — a hot drink made from beans. Example: I drink coffee in the morning.
menu — a list of food and drinks. Example: Can I see the menu, please?
table — a piece of furniture with a flat top. Example: The table by the window is free.
window — an opening in a wall for light and air. Example: The window seat is free.
seat — a place to sit. Example: Is this seat free?
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• What's this? — It's a charger. (asking about a near object)
• What are those? — They're my keys. (asking about far objects)
• There's a big desk and two chairs. (describing a room)
• Is there a dishwasher? — No, there isn't. (asking about a facility)
• A coffee and a croissant, please. (ordering in a cafe)
• The table by the window is free. (using the definite article)
• Can I borrow a pen, please? (polite request)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'a portable computer'?
Which word means 'a cable or device that charges a battery'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use 'there is' and 'there are' to say that something exists or is in a place.

Form:
There is / There are: There is + singular noun. There are + plural noun. Negative: There isn't / There aren't. Question: Is there...? Are there...?

Examples:
• There is a lamp on the desk.
• There are two chairs in the room.
• There isn't a TV in my bedroom.
• Are there any books on the shelf?
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
___ a phone in my bag.
___ three keys on the table.
___ a mirror in the room?
___ any chairs in the kitchen?
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• There is ... (a bed / a lamp / a desk) in my room.
• There are ... (two chairs / three books) on the table.
• There isn't ... (a TV / a mirror) in my bedroom.
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• What is in your bag?
• What is in your room?
• Are there any pictures on your wall?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences with 'there is' about your home.
• Write three sentences with 'there are' about your classroom.
Reading: Everyday Spaces

Modern Studio Apartment — Downtown. Inside, there is a comfortable sofa, a big wooden desk, and two chairs. There is fast Wi-Fi and a small kitchen with a coffee machine. There isn't a dishwasher, and there aren't two bedrooms. The balcony is small, but the view of the park is great. Keys are at the front desk. Ask for Sam.
Is there a dishwasher?
How many chairs are there?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Excuse me, where's the meeting room?
B: It's down the hall on the left, next to the kitchen.
A: Hi! My phone is at two percent. Can I borrow a charger, please?
B: Sure, here you go.
A: Are there any extra chairs in Room B? We have six people today.
B: No, there aren't any in Room B, but there are two near the window.
Where is the meeting room?
Are there extra chairs in Room B?
Speaking task: Put five items on your desk. Quiz your partner with this/these and that/those. Then describe your room with there is/are.

• What's in your bag?
• What's on your desk?
• Is there a balcony in your home?
• What do you order in a cafe?
• How do you ask to borrow something politely?
Role-play: You are in a shared office. Solve three problems: a dead phone, a missing chair, and a request for the meeting room.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write five sentences about your workspace using this/these, there is/are, and one polite request.
Model: This is my ... There is ... There are ... Can I borrow ...?
